strengths: Well-motivated problem: addresses practical challenge of efficient self-verification in sLMs for test-time scaling
Strong empirical results on mathematical reasoning: Llama-3.2 1B with T1 outperforms Llama-3.1 8B on MATH500
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple model scales, benchmarks, verifier types, and detailed ablations
Compelling concept-proof motivation (Figure 1) clearly demonstrating core insight about tools enabling sLM verification
Theoretical contributions: information-theoretic analysis (Theorems 5.1-5.3) providing formal justification for tool integration
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and case studies in appendix
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines established techniques (tool use, distillation, best-of-N) without fundamental innovations
Weak theoretical-practice connection: theory assumes perfect tools, but practice shows ~70% recall in code generation (Table 3)
Critical practical limitation inadequately addressed: low recall (~69-75%) means many correct solutions are rejected with no recovery mechanism
Heavy distillation dependency: method fails without teacher distillation (zero-shot GenRM in Figure 4), reducing claimed efficiency advantage over larger verifiers
Mixed results on knowledge-intensive tasks: MMLU-Pro gains only 5-10% versus 20%+ for MATH, with strong dependence on retrieval quality
Computational costs not analyzed: no timing comparisons despite potentially significant overhead of running tools for 64 solutions
Limited scope: only mathematical and knowledge-QA domains; generalizability to other reasoning tasks unclear
Method fails on specific problem types: ToolV performs worse on Geometry and Level-5 problems (Figure 7) without clear guidance on applicability
Incomplete experimental design: baseline comparison unfair (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama3.1-8B at N=1 only in Figure 3)

strengths: Addresses practical problem of enabling sLMs to self-verify without large model verifiers
Comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro) and verifier types
Provides theoretical analysis via information theory showing tool integration reduces memorization requirements
Honest acknowledgment of limitations (false negatives in code generation, failure cases in appendix)
Demonstrates generalization to both mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks
Strong empirical results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks with careful implementation details provided
weaknesses: Core claim of 'self-verification' is misleading—the method delegates to tools rather than improving model reasoning; this conceptual slippage undermines the paper's central narrative
Limited novelty: applies existing tool-use techniques (PAL, Toolformer) to verification; the two-stage approach (tool filter + RM) is straightforward and incremental
Theory-practice gap: Theorem 5.2 assumes perfect tool use, but Table 3 shows only ~70% recall for code generation, meaning the zero-memorization bound is unachievable in practice

Critical evaluation limitations: code generation achieves only 87% precision and 69% recall; tool-based verifier rejects ~30% of correct solutions as false negatives, severely limiting practical impact

Distillation contribution not isolated: paper relies heavily on knowledge distillation from larger models (gpt-4o-mini or 7B models); unclear how much improvement comes from tools vs. distillation alone
Weak results on non-mathematical tasks: MMLU-Pro improvements are marginal (~44.7% ToolV+PRM vs. 44.0% distilled PRM); only clear gains with perfect gold documents
Non-standard evaluation metrics ('weighted best-of-N') and unfair comparisons (1B+T1 vs. 8B without tools; missing 8B+T1 comparison); different teacher models across experiments confound results
Missing critical ablations: no isolation of ToolV vs. GenRM contributions; no analysis of distillation-only baseline; no sensitivity analysis on code generation hyperparameters
Reproducibility concerns: relies on proprietary models (GPT-4o, Llama); no code release mentioned; distillation requirement negates deployment efficiency claims
Incomplete error analysis: only 2 anecdotal failure examples; no systematic characterization of when/why ToolV fails; no explanation for geometry problem drops or level-5 difficulty dips

strengths: Clear problem identification with well-motivated concept: identifies sLM self-verification as a memorization bottleneck, effectively demonstrated in Figure 1
Strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks: Llama-3.2 1B with T1 outperforms Llama-3.1 8B on MATH500; consistent improvements on GSM8K and MMLU-Pro
Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple model sizes (360M-8B), benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), and verifier types (PRM, GenRM)

Theoretical grounding: Lemma 5.1 and Theorem 5.2 formally demonstrate that tool-based verification reduces memorization requirements from Ω(M³) to 0; Theorem 5.3 connects improved verification to better best-of-N performance
Thorough analysis and ablations: category/difficulty breakdowns (Figure 7), filter analysis (Figure 9), data efficiency (Figure 11), verifier size effects (Figure 8)
Practical implementation and reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, prompts, and experimental setup in appendices; multi-LoRA distillation approach is well-justified
Honest and transparent evaluation: limitations clearly acknowledged; both success and failure cases presented; inconsistencies discussed (e.g., Geometry degradation, Level 5 struggles)
Clean integration with existing verifiers: method works seamlessly with both PRM and GenRM without major architectural changes
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis uses oversimplified toy tasks (checking a+b=c, binary outputs) far from actual MATH problems; guarantees don't directly transfer to empirical settings
Limited method novelty: applying well-established tool-use techniques to self-verification is somewhat incremental; two-stage approach (tool filter + RM scorer) is straightforward

Tool-based verifier limitations: false negatives from low recall (~0.69 for 1B model, Table 3); incorrect code generation causes false rejections (Example F.2); strong assumption of 'explicitly known' tools

Sensitivity to tool quality: MMLU-Pro performance highly unstable with retrieved documents vs. gold documents (Figure 6); method depends critically on document retrieval quality for knowledge-intensive tasks

Limited generalizability: method most effective on math with code interpreters; modest gains on simpler tasks (GSM8K); degrades on hardest problems (Level 5) and specific domains (Geometry); unclear extension to other domains

Incomplete experimental comparisons: baseline comparisons mainly against distilled PRM/GenRM; missing tool-only ablation without distillation; no comparison to other test-time scaling strategies; uses capable teacher (GPT-4o-mini), unclear if approach scales to weaker teachers

Missing critical analyses: computational overhead vs. RM-only baseline not discussed; no error bars or significance testing across random seeds; distillation mechanism unclear (learning correct code vs. when to invoke tools?); experimental hyperparameter choices (4 vs. 8 completions) not justified

Modest improvements in practical settings: while impressive on MATH500, GSM8K improvements are small; MMLU-Pro results are inconsistent across domains; method appears task-dependent rather than universally applicable

strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling proof-of-concept (Figure 1b) clearly demonstrating memorization bottleneck in sLM verification

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), model sizes (360M-8B), and verifier architectures (PRM/GenRM) with strong primary results (1B + ToolV ≥ 8B performance)
Practical framework seamlessly integrates with both generative and process-based verifiers; transparent about computational overhead with honest cost-benefit analysis (Section 6.4)
Thorough ablation studies and analysis including problem-level effects (Figure 6), data efficiency (Figure 15), and necessity of two-stage design (Table 6-7)
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, implementation specifics in appendices, explicit prompts, commitment to code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty: tool use for LLMs is well-established (PAL, Toolformer, CRITIC); contribution of applying tools to sLM verification during test-time scaling feels incremental

Theory-practice disconnect: Lemma 5.1 and Theorem 5.2 analyze only arithmetic (a+b=c) versus complex real problems; Theorem 5.2 assumes perfect tools despite empirical recall of 69-73% (Table 4); Theorem 5.3 addresses binary classification toy setting unconnected to actual verification complexity

Narrow evaluation scope: primary focus on mathematical reasoning (MATH500); MMLU-Pro results in appendix show modest improvements; no evaluation on coding problems, logical reasoning, or non-math domains; knowledge-intensive tasks heavily dependent on retrieval quality

Tool brittleness and domain-specificity: ToolV generates incorrect Python code filtering out correct solutions (Example G.2); Table 4 shows only 69% recall; method requires domain-specific tools (code interpreters, retrievers); unclear generalization without guaranteed tool availability

Incomplete baselines and comparisons: Themis comparison relegated to secondary position; lacking ablations for individual LoRA adapters; no statistical significance testing despite stochastic components; improvements modest on simpler tasks (1-2% on GSM8K)

Missing analysis of critical design choices: no explanation for temperature=0.6, 4 code completions, or sensitivity to these hyperparameters; distillation depends on expensive GPT-4o without sensitivity analysis; edge cases (e.g., all f(x,y)=0) not discussed

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Figure 1(b) compellingly demonstrates that sLMs fail at arithmetic verification while tool augmentation helps
Comprehensive experiments: Multiple models (360M-8B), verifiers (PRM/GenRM), and datasets with extensive ablations in appendices
Practical two-stage design that integrates seamlessly with existing verification approaches
Strong empirical results on math reasoning: Llama-3.2-1B + ToolV > Llama-3.1-8B without ToolV
Honest discussion of computational overhead (Section 6.4) with budget-normalized comparisons (Figures 10-11)
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, prompts in appendices with code release promised
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Applies well-established tool-use techniques (PAL, CRITIC, TORA, Themis) to sLMs in a straightforward way; incremental contribution for top-tier venue

Weak theoretical contributions: Lemma 5.1 applies existing results; Theorem 5.2 is trivial (perfect tool = no memorization); Theorem 5.3 uses toy settings (binary outputs) disconnected from practice; acknowledged gap between theory and practice (C.1)

Fundamental approach limitation: T1 only works as a rejection filter and cannot recover from false negatives (acknowledged limitation); high false negative rate (recall 0.69-0.73 in Table 4) means correct solutions are filtered out

Domain-specific failures: ToolV actually hurts performance on Geometry (Figure 6); only modest improvements on knowledge-intensive tasks (Figure 12: 31%→34% on Health domain); strong dependence on document quality
Generalization concerns: Works well only on calculation-heavy domains; limited evidence of broader applicability; MMLU-Pro results relegated to appendix suggest weak generalization

Computational cost justification incomplete: 1.14× cost trades off simplicity; Figure 11 shows PRM-only is better at small budgets (N≤8); ToolV only helps with large N (N≥16); two-stage pipeline more complex than single larger verifier

Experimental fairness issues: Unclear if baselines (PRM/GenRM) match prior work; different distillation procedures make comparisons problematic; no statistical significance testing or error bars; no ablation on key hyperparameters (e.g., number of code completions)

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem with strong empirical evidence (Figure 1b) that sLMs struggle with memorization-heavy verification tasks

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen-2.5-0.5B, SmolLM2-360M), datasets (MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), and verifier types (PRM, GenRM) with strong results (1B beating 8B model)
Thorough ablations confirming necessity of two-stage design (Tables 6-7), data efficiency (Figure 15), and problem-specific analysis (Figure 6)
Theoretical grounding connecting memorization burden reduction (Lemma 5.1, Theorem 5.2) and verifier improvement (Theorem 5.3) to practical performance
Practical applicability: works with multiple verifier types, uses standard tools, provides detailed implementation details and promises reproducible code release
Honest discussion of limitations and failure modes, with compute budget-normalized analysis (Figure 10) addressing overhead concerns
weaknesses: Limited novelty: applies well-established tool-use paradigm (PAL, CRITIC, ToRA) to sLM verification—contribution is somewhat incremental
Computational overhead not fully resolved: ToolV adds ~1.14× compute (Table 1), and GenRM alone performs better at small test-time budgets (Figure 11), limiting practical advantage
Simplified theoretical results: Section 5.1 toy task (arithmetic) may not generalize; Theorem 5.2 is somewhat tautological; gap between idealized theory and messy practice remains

Tool quality and failure modes underexplored: low recall in code generation (69%, Table 4) means correct solutions are silently filtered; no analysis of threshold selection or strategies to mitigate false negatives
Narrow evaluation scope: heavily weighted toward mathematical reasoning (MATH, GSM8K); MMLU-Pro results inconsistent; no evaluation on domains where tools cannot help

Incomplete ablations: contribution of knowledge distillation vs. tools unclear; multi-LoRA design (Section 4.2) lacks justification; insufficient explanation of performance degradation on Level 5 problems and Geometry category
Missing analysis: no quantified false negative rates, error analysis of tool failures, or guidance on when to trust tool verdicts vs. RM predictions
